scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The skill is essentially documentation for the Adaptyv Bio Foundry public API: a SKILL.md describing authentication, SDK usage, experiment lifecycle, and a bundled endpoint reference. There are no executable scripts, no obfuscation, no hardcoded secrets, no prompt-injection or instruction-override language, no data exfiltration to third-party endpoints (all network references point to the vendor's own documented domains), and the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the documented install/curl workflows. Secret handling guidance is sound (env vars / .env, never hardcode, never commit). Residual risks are limited to supply-chain hygiene (unpinned git install of a beta SDK), an autonomy/financial-commitment concern in the auto-accept-quote example, and minor packaging issues with missing referenced files. Overall the package appears benign.
llm_primary_threats: Autonomous financial commitment via auto-accept quote guidance

findings.title: Documented workflow auto-accepts quotes and creates invoices without user confirmation
findings.description: The instructions present an "Automated Pipeline (Skip Draft + Auto-Accept Quote)" example using `skip_draft: True` and `auto_accept_quote: True`. Per the bundled endpoint reference, accepting a quote finalizes a Stripe quote and creates a draft invoice, i.e. a real financial commitment. Encouraging the agent to use these flags removes the human review checkpoint (Draft → QuoteSent) and could lead to unintended paid lab orders if the agent acts autonomously. No explicit instruction to confirm cost with the user before setting these flags is provided.
findings.snippet:
exp = client.experiments.create({
    "name": "Auto pipeline run",
    "experiment_spec": {...},
    "skip_draft": True,
    "auto_accept_quote": True,
    ...})
findings.remediation: Add an explicit guardrail: require the agent to run `cost-estimate` and obtain explicit user approval before using `skip_draft` or `auto_accept_quote`, and default examples to the Draft + manual quote-confirmation flow.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installed directly from a GitHub repository
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install the `adaptyv-sdk` package directly from a GitHub URL with no version tag, commit hash, or hash verification (`uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"` and `uv add "adaptyv-sdk @ git+..."`). Installing from a mutable default branch means whatever code is on HEAD at install time is executed in the user's environment; a repository compromise or force-push would silently deliver arbitrary code. The package is explicitly described as beta and not on PyPI, so no registry-level provenance checks apply.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
uv add "adaptyv-sdk @ git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
findings.remediation: Pin the dependency to an immutable revision (e.g. `git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git@<tag-or-commit-sha>`), and advise the user to review/approve the install command before execution.

findings.title: Instruction to locate and load .env secret files
findings.description: The skill directs the agent to look for a `.env` file in the project root and load it to obtain the API key. This is standard, benign secret-handling guidance (and the skill correctly forbids hardcoding tokens), but it does broaden the agent's access to a file that commonly contains unrelated credentials. No exfiltration path is present.
findings.snippet: Check for a `.env` file in the project root first; if one exists, use a library like `python-dotenv` to load it.
findings.remediation: Scope the guidance to reading only the `ADAPTYV_API_KEY`/`ADAPTYV_API_URL` variables and instruct the agent never to echo, log, or transmit other values found in `.env`.

findings.title: Referenced files missing from the package

Missing referenced artifacts are a packaging/documentation integrity issue and could cause the agent to search for or fabricate files.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a benign, well-scoped scientific tooling skill. Both bundled Python scripts (admet_report.py, admet_batch.py) use only the standard library (argparse, csv, json, sys, pathlib) with no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no environment variable or credential access, and no reads outside user-supplied input paths. File writes are confined to the user-specified --out-dir (chunk CSVs and manifest.json), consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, and no role redefinition; its guidance is scientifically conservative (rank rather than trust absolute values, flag out-of-domain molecules, do not over-filter). Referenced files are internal to the package and contain only domain documentation. The only dependency guidance is 'pip install admet-ai' from PyPI with a documented version (2.0.1) and license, executed by the user rather than silently by a script — a minor unpinned-install note rather than a supply-chain compromise. Behavior matches the manifest description; no data exfiltration, tool poisoning, obfuscation, or resource-exhaustion patterns were found. Findings are limited to LOW-severity hygiene observations.

While these keywords are all narrowly scoped to the skill's genuine domain (ADMET prediction) and do not impersonate brands or claim general-purpose capability, the explicit activation-priming phrasing is a mild discovery-optimization pattern worth noting. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill is a self-contained, offline computational biology toolkit for antibody variable-domain analysis, and it appears benign. All three Python scripts (number_antibody.py, scan_liabilities.py, physchem_profile.py) restrict themselves to argparse-driven CLI usage, reading FASTA/CSV/TSV files supplied explicitly by the user via Path.read_text, performing pure in-memory regex matching and arithmetic, and writing results to stdout or an explicitly requested --out path. There are no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket), no subprocess/os.system invocations, no eval/exec/compile, no base64 or otherwise obfuscated payloads, no environment-variable harvesting, no access to sensitive paths such as ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or credential stores, no directory walking or bulk collection beyond the files named on the command line, and no hardcoded secrets. The only third-party dependency (anarci, plus HMMER) is imported lazily inside a try/except with a helpful error message; it is a well-known open-source academic package, though it is referenced without a pinned version in the compatibility note. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, safety-bypass, or concealment language; its imperative statements are ordinary domain guidance (state the numbering scheme, pass --regions, do not call a molecule developable from sequence alone) and it explicitly encourages conservative, caveated reporting. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with actual behaviour: the scripts read input files, optionally write an output file, and are invoked from the shell. Bundled reference markdown files are internal to the package and contain only scientific tables and code snippets with no injected instructions or external fetch directives. Cross-component consistency is good: name, description, instructions, and code all describe the same functionality. Only two low-severity, non-exploitable observations were recorded.

findings.title: Description contains an explicit trigger-keyword list
findings.description: The YAML description ends with an enumerated activation keyword list ("Also trigger on antibody, nanobody, VHH, scFv, Fab, CDR, framework, ANARCI, abnumber, IgBLAST, OAS, SAbDab, humanization, Vernier residues, or developability"). This is discovery-optimisation language rather than a functional description. All listed keywords are, however, tightly scoped to the skill's actual domain (antibody sequence numbering, CDR annotation, liability scanning, physicochemical profiling), so there is no capability inflation or brand impersonation and no attempt to claim priority over other skills. Informational only.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on antibody, nanobody, VHH, scFv, Fab, CDR, framework, ANARCI, abnumber, IgBLAST, OAS, SAbDab, humanization, Vernier residues, or developability.
findings.remediation: Optionally trim the keyword enumeration to a concise natural-language description of capability; no security action required.

findings.title: Some referenced documentation paths do not resolve
findings.description: The instruction body links four reference documents (references/numbering-schemes.md, references/developability.md, references/humanization-and-design.md, references/tools.md) which are all present and contain only benign scientific documentation. The additional candidate paths probed under templates/ and assets/ do not exist. This is a documentation/packaging completeness note, not a security exposure: no external URLs are fetched and no instruction tells the agent to execute content found in any file.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: assets/developability.md (not found); templates/tools.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Ensure only existing in-package paths are referenced so the agent does not attempt to resolve missing resources.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The autodock-vina skill is a coherent, domain-specific molecular-docking helper and appears benign. All three Python scripts (make_box.py, dock_batch.py, parse_vina_output.py) use only the standard library, parse local structure/PDBQT files, and invoke external docking binaries (vina, mk_prepare_ligand.py, scrub.py, mk_export.py) via subprocess.run with argument lists — no shell=True, no eval/exec, no dynamic imports, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. There is no network activity, no credential or environment-variable access, no reading of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or other sensitive paths, and no hardcoded secrets. File writes are confined to user-specified output paths (--out, --box-pdb, --out-dir) plus a run_manifest.tsv in the chosen output directory, which is consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) and with the documented purpose. The SKILL.md body and all bundled reference files contain only scientific guidance — no instruction overrides, role redefinition, concealment directives, safety-bypass language, or references to external URLs whose content would be executed. Referenced markdown files are internal to the package (several listed assets/ and templates/ variants simply do not exist, which is a harmless path-resolution artifact). Parallelism is bounded by an explicit --workers argument and each subprocess has a --timeout (default 3600s), so no unbounded resource-exhaustion pattern is present. Only low-severity, informational observations were identified.

findings.title: Broad activation keyword list in skill description
findings.description: The description appends an explicit trigger list ('Also trigger on vina, smina, gnina, mk_prepare_ligand, mk_prepare_receptor, mk_export, scrub.py, PDBQT, autogrid4, docking box, or binding-pose prediction'). The keywords are all tightly scoped to molecular docking and match the skill's actual functionality, so this is normal domain-specific discoverability rather than capability inflation. Noted only for completeness; no over-broad or brand-impersonating claims were found.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on vina, smina, gnina, mk_prepare_ligand, mk_prepare_receptor, mk_export, scrub.py, PDBQT, autogrid4, docking box, or binding-pose prediction.
findings.remediation: No action strictly required; keep the trigger keyword list confined to the skill's true domain, as it currently is.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions in documentation
findings.description: The SKILL.md compatibility field and reference documentation instruct users to install third-party toolchain components (`pip install meeko`, `pip install molscrub`, `pip install vina`, `conda install -c conda-forge vina`, `pip install pdbfixer`) without version pinning or hash verification. The scripts themselves do not perform installs, so this is informational only, but unpinned installs from public registries carry a minor supply-chain risk if a package is compromised or typosquatted.
findings.snippet: conda install -c conda-forge vina, or pip install vina 1.2.7) and Meeko 0.7+ (pip install meeko)
findings.remediation: Pin exact versions (e.g., `pip install meeko==0.7.1 vina==1.2.7 molscrub==<version>`) and prefer verified conda-forge/PyPI sources; note that installation is a user action, not performed automatically by the skill.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The binding-site-analysis skill is a legitimate computational structural-biology utility. All three bundled Python scripts (pocket_report.py, pocket_box.py, site_compare.py) use only the standard library, perform read-only parsing of local fpocket output files (PDB/PQR/_info.txt), and emit results to stdout/stderr. There is no network access, no subprocess/eval/exec usage, no credential or environment-variable access, no obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets. The SKILL.md instructions contain no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; the shell examples shown (grep filtering a PDB, running the fpocket binary) are legitimate, transparent, and consistent with the declared purpose and the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The description's trigger keyword list is domain-specific and proportionate to the stated scope rather than capability inflation. Referenced files that exist (references/fpocket-output.md, references/druggability.md, references/cryptic-and-allosteric.md) are internal to the package and contain only benign scientific documentation; the additional 'not found' paths listed (assets/*, templates/*) are artifacts of path-resolution guessing rather than actual missing dependencies, and their absence poses no security risk. Cross-component behavior matches the manifest claims. No security findings identified.

The `boltz` skill is a legitimate scientific-computing helper for the open-source Boltz-2 cofolding model. All three bundled Python scripts use only the standard library and perform benign, in-scope operations: parsing FASTA/SMILES text files, emitting Boltz input YAML, and aggregating JSON confidence/affinity outputs into a table. There are no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec usage, no credential or environment-variable access, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no filesystem traversal beyond user-supplied paths and the declared output directory. The SKILL.md body and reference documents contain no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; the guidance is scientifically cautious and repeatedly warns about misinterpretation and data-privacy pitfalls. The declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with observed behavior (reading inputs, writing YAML/TSV, invoking the external `boltz` CLI). The description's trailing trigger-keyword list is domain-specific and proportionate to the skill's actual function, not capability inflation. Only two low-severity, informational items were identified: unpinned/dev-branch dependency installation guidance and the documented (and explicitly warned-about) egress of sequences to the public ColabFold MSA server. Overall risk: minimal.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency and direct git installation guidance
findings.description: The reference documentation instructs the user to install Boltz via `pip install boltz` without a version pin, and offers `pip install git+https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz.git` to install the development branch directly from GitHub. Unpinned/HEAD installs mean the code executed on the user's machine can change without review. The repository is the legitimate upstream Boltz project and the risk is low, but the installation guidance provides no version pin or hash verification.
findings.snippet:
pip install boltz            # 2.2.1; requires Python >=3.10,<3.13
# or, for the development version
pip install git+https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz.git
findings.remediation: Pin an explicit version (e.g. `pip install boltz==2.2.1`) and avoid recommending installs from a mutable git HEAD, or note the security implications of doing so.

findings.title: Workflow can transmit user sequences to a public third-party server
findings.description: The documented workflow uses `boltz predict ... --use_msa_server`, which uploads the user's protein sequence to the public ColabFold MSA server. This is inherent to the upstream tool rather than to the skill's own code, and the skill repeatedly and explicitly warns not to use it for confidential or unpublished sequences (in the compatibility field, SKILL.md, running.md, yaml-schema.md, and a runtime reminder printed by make_boltz_yaml.py). Flagged only as informational data-egress awareness; no covert exfiltration exists in the bundled scripts.
findings.snippet: "# reminder: no MSA path given, so `boltz predict` must be run with --use_msa_server (which sends your sequence to the public ColabFold server -- do not use it for confidential sequences)."
findings.remediation: No change required; the existing warnings are adequate. Optionally default guidance to precomputed local MSAs for sensitive targets.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The chembl skill is a well-documented, read-mostly research utility for querying the public ChEMBL REST API. All three scripts use only the Python standard library, perform GET requests exclusively against https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/api/data, and write output only to stdout or a user-specified `--out` file. No evidence was found of prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, environment harvesting), hardcoded secrets, obfuscation/encoded payloads, subprocess/shell execution, eval/exec, dynamic imports, or package installation. URL construction correctly percent-encodes structure queries, filter parsing validates lookup syntax, and file writes use plain `open(..., 'w')` on an explicit user-provided path. The declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` is consistent with running local Python scripts that read references and write TSV/CSV/JSON output; the description accurately matches actual behavior, and the trigger keywords (ChEMBL ids, IC50/Ki/Kd, ebi.ac.uk/chembl) are narrowly scoped to the domain rather than keyword-baiting. Referenced files are internal to the package and contain only legitimate domain documentation; several listed asset/template paths simply do not exist, which is a harmless artifact of path resolution. Only two low-severity, design-inherent observations were noted: an overridable API base URL and unbounded paging volume. Overall the package appears benign.

findings.title: Configurable API base URL allows redirection of queries to arbitrary hosts
findings.description: All bundled scripts expose a `--base-url` flag that overrides the ChEMBL API root. If an agent is influenced by untrusted input (e.g., a user or document instructing it to use a different base URL), query parameters — including SMILES strings, target ids, and other potentially proprietary chemical structures — could be sent to an attacker-controlled host. Default behavior is the legitimate `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/api/data` endpoint, and no credentials are used, so real-world impact is limited to disclosure of query content and potential ingestion of untrusted JSON responses.
findings.snippet:
parser.add_argument("--base-url", default=BASE_URL, help="override the API root (default: the public EBI endpoint)")
...
if path.startswith("http://") or path.startswith("https://"):
    return path
findings.remediation: Optionally restrict `--base-url` to an allowlist of trusted hosts (e.g., *.ebi.ac.uk) or require an explicit environment-variable opt-in, and reject plain http:// schemes.

findings.title: Unbounded paging / large default fetch volumes could consume significant network and CPU resources
findings.description: `paged()` follows `page_meta.next` until exhaustion when no limit is supplied, and `target_activities.py` defaults to `--max-rows 20000` with automatic per-assay-type paging plus batched assay lookups. Combined with a 4-attempt retry loop and exponential backoff (up to 30s sleeps), a broad query could generate many hundreds of HTTP requests and long-running execution. Retries are bounded and there is a safety cap, so this is informational rather than a genuine DoS primitive.
findings.snippet:
parser.add_argument("--max-rows", type=int, default=20000, help="safety cap on rows fetched")
...
while path:
    document = get(path, ...)
findings.remediation: Document expected request volumes and consider a global request-count ceiling plus a wall-clock timeout for paging loops.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The chemical-space skill is a well-documented, benign chemoinformatics helper. Its two scripts use only the Python standard library, perform read-only unauthenticated HTTPS GETs against a single well-known public service (cartblanche.docking.org) for public compound identifiers, and otherwise do pure arithmetic on tranche naming and screening-cascade cost estimation. There is no eval/exec, no subprocess or shell invocation, no file writes, no credential or environment harvesting beyond a single endpoint override variable, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no dependency installation. Network retries are bounded (MAX_ATTEMPTS=4, capped 30s backoff), so no DoS/compute-exhaustion pattern exists. The SKILL.md body and all three bundled reference documents contain no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language in any language — they are domain guidance with unusually candid caveats. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are broader than what the scripts require but are not violated. Only minor hygiene issues were found: a keyword trigger list in the description, an environment-variable-overridable base URL, and several dangling references to non-existent templates/ and assets/ files.

findings.title: Keyword-heavy description for discovery triggering
findings.description: The YAML description ends with an explicit trigger keyword list ('Also trigger on ZINC22, CartBlanche, Enamine REAL, make-on-demand, tangible library, synthon, tranche, giga-scale enumeration, or ultra-large virtual screening.'). While all keywords are topically consistent with the skill's actual chemoinformatics purpose and not over-broad or brand-impersonating, the pattern is a mild form of activation keyword stuffing worth noting. No capability inflation was detected — the scripts do exactly what the description claims.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on ZINC22, CartBlanche, Enamine REAL, make-on-demand, tangible library, synthon, tranche, giga-scale enumeration, or ultra-large virtual screening.
findings.remediation: Keep the description to a natural-language statement of purpose; trigger keyword lists are acceptable but should remain narrowly scoped to the domain, as they are here.

findings.title: Missing referenced files (templates/ and assets/ variants)
findings.description: Several referenced paths (templates/zinc22-and-cartblanche.md, templates/screening-strategy.md, templates/combinatorial-spaces.md, assets/*.md) do not exist in the package. The three genuinely referenced files under references/ are present and benign. Missing paths are a documentation/packaging hygiene issue rather than a security threat, but dangling references could later be satisfied by attacker-supplied files of the same name.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: templates/zinc22-and-cartblanche.md (not found); assets/combinatorial-spaces.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Remove stale path references or ship the referenced files inside the skill package so resolution cannot fall through to unexpected locations.

findings.title: Base URL overridable via environment variable and CLI flag
findings.description: The HTTP base URL is read from the CARTBLANCHE_URL environment variable and can also be overridden by the --base-url CLI flag. If an attacker can set that environment variable in the agent's environment, lookups would be redirected to an arbitrary host, sending ZINC identifiers (non-sensitive) there and returning attacker-controlled JSON that would be rendered into the agent's context. Impact is low: only public compound identifiers are transmitted, no credentials or local files are read, and responses are parsed as JSON rather than executed.
findings.snippet: BASE_URL = os.environ.get("CARTBLANCHE_URL", "https://cartblanche.docking.org")
findings.remediation: Optionally validate that the resolved base URL uses HTTPS and belongs to an allowlist of expected hosts (e.g. *.docking.org), and log the effective endpoint when it differs from the default.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The clinicaltrials skill is a well-documented, read-only research wrapper around the public ClinicalTrials.gov v2 REST API. All three scripts use only the Python standard library, perform GET requests to a single public registry endpoint, and print tabulated results to stdout/stderr. There is no eval/exec, no subprocess or shell invocation, no filesystem traversal, no reading of credential stores or environment secrets, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no outbound POST/upload of any local data. The SKILL.md body and the bundled reference files contain domain guidance only, with no instruction-override, concealment, role-redefinition, or jailbreak language, and the reference files read are internal to the package (several alternate paths listed as 'not found' are simply resolver noise). Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are broader than what the scripts actually need but are not violated. Findings are limited to low-severity hygiene items: keyword-baiting in the description, an environment-variable-overridable API base URL, and unbounded paging that can generate many outbound requests. Overall the skill appears benign and behaves consistently with its stated purpose.

findings.title: API base URL overridable via environment variable and CLI flag
findings.description: The HTTP base URL is read from the CTGOV_API_URL environment variable and can also be overridden with --base-url. If an attacker (or a poisoned environment) sets this variable, requests intended for clinicaltrials.gov would be sent to an arbitrary host, redirecting query terms and returning attacker-controlled JSON that is then summarised into the agent's context. No credentials or local files are transmitted, and only query parameters (condition, drug, sponsor names) are sent, so exposure impact is low. Note _build_url also returns a raw path unchanged when it starts with http(s)://, though no code path currently supplies user-controlled absolute URLs.
findings.snippet:
BASE_URL = os.environ.get("CTGOV_API_URL", "https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2")
...
if path.startswith("http://") or path.startswith("https://"):
    return path
findings.remediation: Pin the base URL to the official HTTPS registry host by default, validate any override against an allowlist of trusted hosts, and reject non-HTTPS schemes.

findings.title: Keyword-baiting phrases appended to skill description
findings.description: The description ends with an explicit trigger-word list ("Also trigger on ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT number, trial registry, study phase, enrolment, primary outcome measure, recruiting status, trial sponsor, or competitive landscape"). This increases activation likelihood via keyword stuffing. However, all listed keywords are directly relevant to the skill's genuine function (querying the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API), so the practical risk is minimal and there is no capability inflation beyond the actual scope.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT number, trial registry, study phase, enrolment, primary outcome measure, recruiting status, trial sponsor, or competitive landscape.
findings.remediation: Optionally trim the explicit trigger-keyword list to a concise natural-language description of scope.

findings.title: Paged API walking can issue large numbers of outbound requests
findings.description: ct_landscape.py and ct_search.py page through matching studies with a cursor, and count commands issue one total_count request per phase/status value. With a large --limit and a broad condition this can result in many sequential HTTPS requests plus exponential backoff sleeps (up to 30s each, 4 attempts). Defaults are bounded (limit 50-200, pageSize<=1000) and the skill documentation explicitly warns to use --limit deliberately, so this is a mild resource-consumption consideration rather than an intentional DoS pattern.
findings.snippet: rows = [summarise(study) for study in paged(params, limit=args.limit, base_url=args.base_url)]
findings.remediation: Consider capping --limit to a sane maximum and adding a total request budget to prevent accidental heavy polling of the public registry.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The datamol skill is a documentation-only cheminformatics helper: SKILL.md plus six reference markdown files, with no Python or Bash scripts bundled. All code shown is illustrative, idiomatic datamol/RDKit usage (SMILES parsing, standardization, descriptors, fingerprints, clustering, scaffolds, fragmentation, conformers, visualization, reactions). No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or system-prompt extraction attempts were found in any language. There is no eval/exec, subprocess, os.system, reverse shell, network POST, credential file access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), environment harvesting, base64/hex obfuscation, or hardcoded secret anywhere in the package. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the documented behavior (file I/O for SDF/CSV/XLSX and pip installs) and are not exceeded. The description is verbose and includes explicit trigger tokens (dm.to_mol, dm.cluster_mols, etc.), but these are narrowly scoped to the datamol library and the skill defers to sibling skills (rdkit, medchem, molfeat) rather than making over-broad general-assistant claims, so this is legitimate routing rather than capability inflation. Cloud/HTTPS I/O via fsspec is the only data-egress surface, and the skill proactively gates it behind explicit user request and destination confirmation while scoping credentials to provider-specific variables. Only low-severity hygiene items were identified: unpinned pip installs and dangling reference-path artifacts. Overall risk: LOW — the package appears benign and behaviorally consistent with its stated purpose.

findings.title: Documented cloud I/O paths use provider credentials from the environment
findings.description: The skill documents remote read/write via fsspec (s3://, gs://, https://), which implicitly uses provider credentials from environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS). This is a legitimate library feature and the skill explicitly instructs that cloud paths should only be used when the user requests them, that write destinations must be confirmed, that credential scope should be limited to provider variables, and that no environment data is transmitted to third parties. No exfiltration endpoint, no credential reading code, and no automated upload behavior is present — flagged only as an informational data-egress surface for the operator to be aware of.
findings.snippet:
dm.save_df(df, "s3://bucket/output.parquet")  # confirm destination first
"Cloud backends read credentials from the standard provider environment (for example AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID ...). Datamol passes these to fsspec locally; it does not collect or transmit environment variables to third-party endpoints."
findings.remediation: No change strictly required. Optionally reiterate that the agent must obtain explicit user confirmation before any remote write and must never echo credential values into chat or logs.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install packages via `uv pip install datamol`, `uv pip install s3fs`, and `uv pip install gcsfs` without version pinning or hash verification. While these are well-known, legitimate PyPI packages from a reputable maintainer (datamol-io/Valence Labs), unpinned installs mean the resolved artifact is whatever is current at install time, which is a minor supply-chain exposure. No typosquatting or untrusted GitHub sources are used.
findings.snippet:
```bash
uv pip install datamol
```
... `uv pip install s3fs`   # AWS S3 ... `uv pip install gcsfs`  # Google Cloud Storage
findings.remediation: Recommend pinned versions consistent with the documented tested release (e.g., `uv pip install "datamol==0.12.5"`) and note that installation should be user-approved.

findings.title: Broken/non-existent file references in extracted reference list
findings.description: The reference extraction lists several paths that do not exist in the package (assets/*.md, templates/*.md, sklearn.py, datamol.py). Inspection shows these are artifacts of pattern extraction: the six real reference documents exist under references/ and are present; `sklearn.py` and `datamol.py` originate from `import datamol as dm` / `from sklearn.ensemble import ...` code snippets, and the SKILL.md explicitly clarifies these are third-party PyPI packages, not bundled scripts. Impact is documentation hygiene only, but dangling references could later be satisfied by an attacker-dropped file of the same name in the skill directory.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: sklearn.py (not found); Referenced File: datamol.py (not found); Referenced File: assets/core_api.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Keep all reference links limited to the actual references/ directory paths and avoid phrasing that causes import statements to be parsed as local file references.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The deepchem skill is a legitimate, documentation-heavy molecular machine-learning helper. All three bundled Python scripts use argparse-driven, well-scoped DeepChem APIs for featurization, dataset splitting, model training and evaluation. There is no eval/exec, no os.system or subprocess usage, no shell interpolation of user input, no credential or environment-variable access, no filesystem traversal beyond user-specified CSV paths, and no outbound network calls other than standard package installs and public HuggingFace/MoleculeNet dataset downloads. No prompt injection, concealment directives, role redefinition, or instruction-override language appears in SKILL.md or in the bundled reference markdown; the reference files contain only ordinary DeepChem code examples. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the observed behavior (training scripts write model directories and install packages), and the description accurately matches script functionality, including honest cross-references to sibling skills. Remaining observations are low-severity hygiene issues: unpinned/git-branch dependency installation, unpinned remote pretrained-model downloads, and a few dangling documentation paths.
llm_primary_threats: Unverified remote pretrained model artifact download

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation and install directly from a Git branch
findings.description: The SKILL.md installation instructions tell the agent to run `uv pip install deepchem`, `uv pip install --pre deepchem`, and `pip install git+https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem.git` without version pinning or hash verification. Installing an untagged build from the default branch of a GitHub repository means the exact code executed is not reproducible and could change between runs. The instructions also suggest `conda install "mkl<2025"`. This is standard practice for scientific Python tooling and the repository is the legitimate upstream project, so the risk is limited, but it is an unverified supply-chain path.
findings.snippet: pip install git+https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem.git  ...  uv pip install --pre deepchem  ...  uv pip install 'deepchem[torch]'
findings.remediation: Pin explicit versions (e.g. `deepchem==2.8.0`) and prefer tagged releases over installing from a mutable Git branch; document that nightly/git installs are unverified builds.

findings.title: Several referenced documentation paths do not exist in the package
findings.description: The instructions/reference resolution list includes files under templates/ and assets/ (e.g. templates/api_reference.md, assets/workflows.md, assets/core_capabilities.md) that are not present in the skill package. Missing references can cause the agent to search elsewhere or fabricate content, but there is no evidence of malicious intent — the actual reference documents exist under references/.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: templates/api_reference.md (not found); Referenced File: assets/workflows.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Remove or correct stale reference paths so all referenced files resolve inside the skill directory.

findings.title: Automatic download and execution of third-party pretrained model weights
findings.description: The transfer_learning.py script instantiates HuggingFace models by remote identifier ('seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1', 'ibm/MoLFormer-XL-both-10pct') and GroverModel with a local model_dir, causing weights/tokenizer configs to be fetched from the HuggingFace Hub at runtime without pinned revisions or checksum verification. Loading remote model artifacts can execute arbitrary deserialization code depending on the backend. These are well-known public model repositories and the behavior is disclosed in the skill documentation, so severity is low.
findings.snippet: 'model_id': 'seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1' ... 'model_id': 'ibm/MoLFormer-XL-both-10pct' ... model = dc.models.HuggingFaceModel(model=PRETRAINED_MODELS['chemberta']['model_id'], ...)

...

findings.remediation: Only attach `api_key` when the resolved host matches an allowlist (e.g. `api.fda.gov`), and warn on stderr when a non-default base URL is used.

findings.title: Unvalidated identifiers interpolated into download URLs (path traversal / SSRF surface)
findings.description: fetch_structure.py builds download URLs by interpolating user-supplied PDB ids, assembly numbers, accessions, and component ids directly into f-strings without validating character sets (e.g. f"{RCSB_FILES}/{pdb_id}.{suffix}"). Because the host prefix is a hardcoded constant, a crafted identifier containing '../' or '@' could at most redirect the request to another path on files.rcsb.org, and the AlphaFold branch fetches URLs returned by the AlphaFold API (server-controlled) and writes them to a local file whose name comes from the remote URL basename. No credentials, environment variables, or local sensitive files are read, and no data is sent outward, so real-world risk is low.
